records.summary: The records show 500 Castro Street sits in the Castro Street NCD where a bar use is conditional and requires a CUA; the pathway confirms this is a change of use from an existing restaurant (an active Type 47 license is on file). The site history reveals a long-running restaurant/bar at this address (Harvey's), with two CUAs approved in the late 1990s for live entertainment at the same parcel (1996.576C and 1998.034C, which amended entertainment hours to midnight). The block is saturated: 38 food and drink businesses within 500 feet, including 12 bars, and 28 active on-sale ABC licenses within 500 feet (46 within 1,000 feet)—a density that flags undue concentration. Only two dated use decisions for comparable concepts were found nearby in the last ten years, both approved, but the count is too small to show a rate. The nearest comparable precedent is a 1999 CUA approving dancing at Badlands (30m away), and several bars on the block have POE permits for live entertainment, most with conditions limiting hours.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) authorizing dancing at Badlands, an existing bar 30 meters away on 18th Street in the Castro NCD, approved in 1999. This is the closest comparable nightclub use in the district.
comparables.key_takeaway: Dancing in a bar requires a CUA in the Castro NCD. The Commission approved dancing at an existing bar on this block, establishing that nightclub uses are permissible with conditional use authorization even in this saturated corridor.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) approving a Place of Entertainment permit as accessory to an established bar (The Edge) 68 meters away on 18th Street in the Castro NCD, decided in 2012. This is a bar adding live entertainment.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved a POE for an existing bar on this block, confirming that entertainment uses accessory to bars are approvable with a CUA in the Castro NCD despite the corridor's density.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) at the subject property itself (4109-4111 18th / 500 Castro) modifying a prior CUA to limit live entertainment hours to midnight in a restaurant/bar, approved in 1998. This modified the 1996 approval at this same site.
comparables.key_takeaway: At this exact parcel, the Commission previously approved live entertainment in a restaurant/bar but conditioned entertainment to end at midnight (not 2 a.m.), suggesting sensitivity to late-night impacts at 500 Castro even with prior entertainment authorization.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) at the subject property (4109-4111 18th / 500 Castro) originally approving live entertainment in the Castro NCD in 1996. This was the first entertainment authorization at this parcel.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved live entertainment at this site in 1996, establishing precedent for entertainment use at 500 Castro, but the subsequent 1998 amendment limiting hours to midnight signals the Commission may restrict late-night entertainment at this location.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (miscellaneous permit) at the subject property (500 Castro / 4109-4111 18th) denied in 1996 for lack of conditional use authorization. This denial predated the successful CUA filing by three months.
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning denied a place of entertainment permit at this exact parcel in 1996 because no CUA had been obtained, confirming that entertainment and dancing are not permitted by right and require Commission approval at 500 Castro.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) denied in 1994 for extended hours of operation at an existing bar 98 meters away at 465-469 Castro Street in the Castro NCD. This is the only outright denial among the nearby bar/entertainment cases.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission denied extended operating hours for a bar in the Castro NCD in 1994, demonstrating that late-night operations are not automatically granted and that the Commission will deny bar-use requests it finds inappropriate for the corridor.

comparables.why_comparable: Agency referral (miscellaneous permit) at 4146 18th Street (77m away) in 2005 approving a bar as a nonconforming use but explicitly stating dancing is not permitted without a CUA. This is a comparable bar location on the same block.
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning approved a bar with recorded music and games but explicitly prohibited dancing without a CUA, reinforcing that dancing is not permitted as an ancillary activity in Castro NCD bars and requires separate conditional use authorization.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (miscellaneous permit) at 4146-4150 18th Street (77m away) in 2008 approving a bar with recorded music but stating 'DANCING IS NOT PERMITTED' without a CUA. Same location as MB0500058, reiterating the prohibition.
comparables.key_takeaway: Three years after the prior decision at this same bar, Planning again approved recorded music and games but prohibited dancing without a CUA, confirming the consistent policy that dancing requires conditional use authorization in the Castro NCD.

comparables.why_comparable: Agency referral (miscellaneous permit) at 4067 18th Street (76m away) in 2011 recommending approval of a POE for an existing bar under Planning Code § 715.48, which allows existing bars to obtain POE permits without additional CU if they demonstrate regular entertainment operation.
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning approved a POE for an existing bar under the § 715.48 exemption, which allows bars that have been regularly operating as entertainment venues to get POE permits without a new CUA. This pathway does not apply to new bars or changes of use like this concept.

comparables.why_comparable: Use decision (CUA) approved in 2020 for a restaurant with Type 41 beer/wine license 59 meters away at 4092 18th Street in the Castro NCD, conditioned to operate 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. Recent approval showing Commission approach to late-night food/beverage uses.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved 2 a.m. closing hours for a restaurant with alcohol service on this block in 2020, demonstrating that late-night operations to 2 a.m. are approvable in the Castro NCD for food and beverage uses, subject to standard noise and maintenance conditions.

patterns.pattern: Dancing in bars and nightclubs is a conditional use in the Castro NCD and consistently requires a CUA; Planning routinely denied or prohibited dancing when no CUA was in place.

Entertainment uses at 500 Castro (the subject parcel) have been approved by the Commission in the past (1996, 1998), but entertainment hours were limited to midnight rather than 2 a.m., even for a restaurant/bar with food service.

The Commission approved multiple POE and entertainment permits for bars on the 18th Street corridor in the Castro NCD during the 1999-2012 period, establishing that entertainment-oriented bar uses are permissible with proper authorization.

Recent CUAs in the Castro NCD for food and beverage uses have been approved with 2 a.m. closing hours and standard conditions addressing noise, sidewalk maintenance, and a community liaison, but without additional entertainment-specific restrictions.

The Commission denied at least one request for extended hours at a bar in the Castro NCD (1994), and Planning has consistently stated that certain activities (dancing, extended hours) require CU authorization and are not granted automatically.

Planning Code § 715.48 allows existing bars that have been regularly operating as entertainment venues to obtain POE permits without a new CUA, but this exemption does not apply to new bar uses or changes of use from restaurant to bar/nightclub.

approvals.summary: A bar use at 3,172 sq ft with dancing and nighttime entertainment requires a Conditional Use Authorization in the Castro NCD per Planning Code § 715; the concept is a change of use from restaurant and the formula retail question is not decided.

findings.text: Planning Code § 715 makes a bar on the first story a conditional use in the Castro NCD (in force from March 2022). Nighttime entertainment and uses over 2,000 sq ft also trigger conditional use. The concept at 3,172 sq ft meets all three triggers.
An active ABC Type 47 license (on-sale general, eating place) is on file at 500 Castro Street for Harvey's, issued June 2015, establishing the existing use as a restaurant.

Restaurant to bar and nighttime entertainment is a change of use under Planning Code § 102. Neighborhood notification under § 311 is required because the new use is not principally permitted in the Castro NCD.

The Planning Commission approved a CUA for dancing at Badlands bar, 30 meters away on 18th Street in the Castro NCD, in 1999 (filed June 1999, approved August 1999 in 63 days). This is the nearest comparable nightclub approval.

At this same parcel, the Commission previously approved live entertainment in a restaurant/bar in 1996 (case 1996.576C) but later amended the CUA in 1998 (case 1998.034C) to limit entertainment hours to midnight rather than 2 a.m., indicating past sensitivity to late-night impacts at 500 Castro.

The description does not state whether the business is part of a chain that shares its name, look or menu, so the formula retail trigger under § 715 is not decided and the CUA status rests on the other three triggers.

approvals.summary: The alcohol license status is insufficient information because the concept does not specify beer/wine or full liquor service, nor whether a new license will be issued or an existing license transferred; both affect timeline, cost and local approvals.

findings.text: ABC will refer any original or transfer application to the San Francisco Police Department (ABC Liaison Unit) and to the Planning Department for zoning sign-off before issuing or transferring a license.

Within 500 feet of this address there are 28 active on-sale ABC licenses (46 within 1,000 feet), flagging potential undue concentration. The census tract count is not shown because three licenses' status on November 20, 2023 is unknown.

A Type 48 full-liquor bar license is a quota license acquired by purchase and transfer, typically $100,000–$450,000 in San Francisco; transfers take 90–240 days including escrow, posting and local sign-off per the ABC catalog entry.

A Type 42 beer-and-wine bar license is non-quota and issued directly by ABC in 60–150 days, but nearly every city requires a conditional use permit before ABC will issue, so the local hearing is the long pole.

approvals.summary: A Place of Entertainment permit is required for dancing, live entertainment and amplified sound; the Entertainment Commission holds a public hearing and routes the application to Police, Planning, DBI, Public Health and Fire for review.

findings.text: Police Code § 1023 required a dance permit on November 20, 2023 to conduct dancing unless a valid Place of Entertainment permit was held. Police Code § 1060 et seq. governs POE, Limited Live Performance and Fixed Place Outdoor Amplified Sound permits.

A POE application is sent to the Police Department, Planning, DBI, Public Health and Fire for review (Police Code § 1060.2(b)). The 2026–27 application fee is $2,708 and the permit requires a 30-day posted notice and a Commission hearing.

In 2012 the Commission approved a CUA for a Place of Entertainment as accessory to an existing bar at The Edge, 68 meters away on 18th Street in the Castro NCD (filed March 2012, approved June 2012 in 105 days).

Planning Code § 715.48 allows existing bars in the Castro NCD that have been regularly operating as entertainment venues to obtain POE permits without a new CUA if the Entertainment Commission is satisfied they meet the criteria. This exemption does not apply to a change of use from restaurant to bar/nightclub.

approvals.summary: A health permit to operate is allowed (issued after plan check and inspection without a hearing) for a bar serving beverages; the application routes to Planning for zoning review.

findings.text: A food or drink business needs a health permit to operate under the California Retail Food Code and San Francisco Health Code Article 8. The permit is issued after plan check and final inspection without a discretionary hearing.
The Department of Public Health permit application for a bar or beverage facility is sent to the Planning Department for zoning review per the Interagency Permit Referrals guidelines.

approvals.summary: A building permit with change of use is further review; the concept is a Planning Code change of use from restaurant to bar, and a building permit must conform to the Planning Code before DBI issues it, so the permit depends on the CUA.

findings.text: Restaurant to bar and nighttime entertainment is a change of use under Planning Code § 102, and an active Type 47 license on file at 500 Castro Street establishes the existing restaurant use.

The California Building Code classifies a restaurant or bar as Assembly Group A-2, and a space for fewer than 50 people as Group B. The concept does not state the occupant load, so the proposed Building Code occupancy group is not established.

The existing Building Code occupancy group of the space is not in public records; only plans or a DBI inspection show it. Whether a change of occupancy under the Building Code is required is not established.

San Francisco Building Code § 106A.1 requires a building permit for a change of use, and Planning Code § 175 requires the permit to conform to the Planning Code before DBI issues it. The building permit is routed to Planning for zoning review.

The concept states it will merge three storefronts (500, 506, 508 Castro Street). Merging storefronts typically triggers Planning zoning review and neighborhood notification under § 311/312 because it is a physical change affecting the streetscape.

expected_conditions.condition: Hours of operation limited to 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. seven days a week, with entertainment ending earlier (possibly midnight) as imposed in the 1998 CUA at this parcel.
expected_conditions.basis: The 2020 CUA at 4092 18th Street (59m away) conditioned a restaurant/bar to 6 a.m.–2 a.m. (case 2019-021378CUA). The 1998 CUA at this same parcel (500 Castro) limited entertainment to midnight, not 2 a.m., suggesting the Commission may restrict late-night entertainment here even if bar hours run to 2 a.m.

expected_conditions.condition: Soundproofing or insulation for noise so that incidental noise is not audible beyond the premises or in other sections of the building, and fixed-source equipment noise does not exceed decibel levels in the Noise Control Ordinance.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition in recent CUAs for eating and drinking uses (e.g., 2019-021378CUA condition on soundproofing). POE permits routinely require acoustic reports and soundproofing plans for venues with amplified sound and dancing.

expected_conditions.condition: Maintain the main entrance and sidewalks abutting the property in a clean condition, and daily monitor the sidewalk within a one-block radius to keep it free of litter associated with the business during business hours.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition in recent CUAs for eating and drinking uses (2019-021378CUA) per Police Code Article 1, Section 34 and DPW Street and Sidewalk Maintenance Standards.

expected_conditions.condition: Appoint a community liaison officer to address concerns of nearby owners and occupants; provide written notice of the liaison's name, address and phone number to the Zoning Administrator and registered neighborhood groups.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition in recent CUAs (2019-021378CUA). Given the density of bars on this corridor and the history of entertainment at 500 Castro, the Commission will likely require ongoing neighbor communication.

expected_conditions.condition: Security plan and ID-check procedures at the door, with trained security staff on site during entertainment hours, as required by the Entertainment Commission for POE permits.
expected_conditions.basis: POE permits for nightclubs and bars with dancing routinely carry conditions requiring security plans, ID checks and capacity monitoring. The 1999 CUA for dancing at Badlands (30m away) and the 2012 CUA at The Edge (68m away) both involved entertainment uses that would have been conditioned by the Entertainment Commission.

expected_conditions.condition: Capacity limit tied to the Fire Department Place of Assembly permit (if occupant load is 50 or more) and posted occupancy sign; no occupancy beyond the posted limit.
expected_conditions.basis: Fire Department regulations require a Place of Assembly permit and posted occupancy sign for venues with occupant loads of 50 or more (catalog entry sf.fire_place_of_assembly). The Entertainment Commission cross-references this permit for POE applications.

expected_conditions.condition: Compliance with Planning Code § 202.2(a)(6) for alcohol sales: all advertising and signage placed to ensure law enforcement has a clear and unobstructed view of the interior, including the cash register area, from the exterior sidewalk or entrance.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition in recent CUAs involving alcohol (2019-021378CUA, 2021-005099CUA for a bottle shop 65m away). Section 202.2(a)(6)(A) requires transparency for law enforcement visibility.

filing_playbook.action: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at the Secretary of State's bizfile portal. Once the entity is registered, apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) online at irs.gov (issued immediately). The lease, bank account, Business Registration and all city permits require the entity name and EIN. File the Statement of Information within 90 days ($20 LLC, $25 corporation).

filing_playbook.action: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Registration Certificate and Business Account Number (BAN).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply online with the entity name, EIN and business description within 30 days of starting business. Fee is tiered by gross receipts (e.g., $55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, plus $4 state fee for 2026–27). The BAN is required for every other city permit (Planning, Health, Entertainment, DBI). File a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the entity name, publish it in a court-approved newspaper for four weeks, and file proof of publication within 45 days.

filing_playbook.action: Schedule a pre-application meeting with the San Francisco Planning Department to discuss the CUA pathway, the history of entertainment approvals at 500 Castro, storefront merger, neighborhood notification and the formula retail question.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Request a pre-application meeting with a planner assigned to the Castro NCD. Explain the concept: a nightclub with dancing, live entertainment and amplified sound, closing at 2 a.m., merging three storefronts (500, 506, 508 Castro) from an existing restaurant use. Disclose the 1996 and 1998 CUAs at this parcel that approved entertainment to midnight and ask whether the Commission will condition entertainment hours differently for a nightclub versus a restaurant. Ask whether the storefront merger triggers additional review, what the neighborhood notification radius is, and confirm that the bar use, nighttime entertainment and 3,172 sq ft size all require CU. Confirm whether the business is formula retail (chain) or independent.

filing_playbook.action: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with the San Francisco Planning Department, including the project description, floor plans, neighborhood outreach plan and signed lease or letter of intent for 500 Castro Street.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the CUA application online through the Planning Department portal with the BAN, property address, entity name and a project description stating: 'Request Conditional Use Authorization under Planning Code § 303 to establish a bar use with nighttime entertainment (dancing, live entertainment, amplified sound) in the Castro NCD at 500 Castro Street (3,172 sq ft), converting from restaurant use (existing Type 47 license on file). Use triggers: bar on first story, nighttime entertainment, and use size over 2,000 sq ft per § 715. The business is [independent / part of a chain with fewer than 11 locations / formula retail]. Hours: 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. The project merges three storefronts and requires neighborhood notification.' Attach floor plans, an operations narrative describing security, capacity, noise control and good-neighbor measures, and evidence of community outreach (meeting with…

filing_playbook.action: Obtain a California Seller's Permit from CDTFA (required before ABC will accept a liquor license application) and register for employer payroll taxes with EDD.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register online at the CDTFA online services portal for a seller's permit (free, often issued the same day). ABC will not issue a liquor license until the seller's permit exists. If you will have employees, register as an employer with EDD's e-Services for Business within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages in a quarter (free, takes 1–7 days). Arrange workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund before the first employee starts; several city permits ask for proof of coverage.

filing_playbook.action: After the CUA is approved by the Planning Commission (and the 30-day appeal period expires), file the ABC license application: either a new Type 42 (beer/wine bar) or purchase and escrow an existing Type 48 (full-liquor bar) and file a transfer application.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: For a Type 42 beer-and-wine bar license (non-quota, issued directly by ABC, typical timeline 60–150 days, ABC fee approximately $1,000–$1,600): Apply online at ABC's portal with the seller's permit number, entity documents, signed lease, and a copy of the Planning Commission CUA approval. ABC will send the application to SFPD and Planning for sign-off, post a 30-day public notice at the premises, and issue the license if no protests or undue concentration objections are sustained. For a Type 48 full-liquor bar license (quota license typically purchased for $100,000–$450,000 in San Francisco, transfer timeline 90–240 days): Engage a license broker to locate an available Type 48, negotiate a purchase agreement and open escrow. File a person-to-person and premises-to-premises transfer application with ABC, attaching the CUA approval, and the same referral, posting and waiting period applie…

filing_playbook.action: After the CUA is approved, file the Place of Entertainment permit application with the San Francisco Entertainment Commission, including the security plan, sound mitigation plan and proof of CUA approval.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Email the Entertainment Commission Deputy Director to confirm zoning eligibility and that the CUA covers the POE use. Submit the POE application online with the BAN, lease or temporary liquor license, a security and operations plan (ID checks, trained security staff, capacity monitoring, incident log), and a sound mitigation plan (acoustic report, soundproofing measures, amplifier limits). The $2,708 application fee (2026–27) is due at filing. The Commission will route the application to Police, Planning, DBI, Public Health and Fire for review and require a 30-day posted notice at the premises (yellow notice visible from the public right-of-way). The Commission holds a public hearing (1st and 3rd Tuesdays) to consider the permit and approve conditions addressing hours, sound, security and neighbor communication. If the occupant load is 50 or more, obtain the Fire Department Place of Ass…

filing_playbook.action: File the building permit application with the Department of Building Inspection for tenant improvements, storefront merger and change of use, attaching the CUA approval and stamped architectural plans.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Hire a California-licensed architect to prepare plans for the tenant improvements (storefront merger, bar layout, ADA restrooms, egress, soundproofing, lighting) and stamp them. Submit the building permit application online through DBI's permit tracking system with the BAN, the CUA approval (or a pending CUA case number if DBI allows pre-submittal), and the stamped plans. The application routes to Planning for zoning conformance review under § 175, and to other departments (DPH if any plumbing or sinks, Fire if sprinkler or hood work). Fees are a percentage of construction valuation (typically $800–$15,000 for a bar TI). Electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are pulled by licensed subcontractors. Plan for 14–120 days depending on plan completeness and the scope of work. Schedule the final inspection after construction and before opening; DBI will not issue a certificate of occupan…

timeline_cost.notes: The day and cost ranges cover the approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000), Place of Entertainment permit (45–120 days, $2,708–$3,800), health permit to operate (14–45 days, $470–$1,000 for FY2026–27), and building permit with change of use (14–120 days, $800–$15,000). The ranges are times to approval, not to denial or withdrawal. The CUA is the long pole (6–10 months including pre-application, environmental review, neighborhood notice and hearing scheduling). The cost does not include the ABC license: a Type 42 beer/wine bar is approximately $1,000–$1,600 in ABC fees and takes 60–150 days; a Type 48 full-liquor bar is typically purchased for $100,000–$450,000 (license purchase price plus transfer fees) and takes 90–240 days including escrow. Undue concentration in the census tract (46 ABC licenses within 1,000 ft) may add 1–3 months if a Public Convenience or Necessity finding is required. The figures do not include soft costs (architect, acoustic consultant, legal, broker), construction (tenant improvements to merge storefronts, soundproofing, ADA, bar build-out), or pre-opening operating expenses during the entitlement period.
